entry.title: Why cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to India
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Why cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to IndiaWhy cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to India

Income should be taxed on the same principle, whether it comes from labour or capital beyond ideology

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTThe finance minister has indicated the government’s willingness to re-examine India’s long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax on equity, driven largely by the need to attract foreign investors at a time when the rupee and the balance of payments (BoP) are under pressure. It should do no such thing. Our capital gains tax regime is broadly on the right trajectory, with tax rates on gains from different types of assets converging. The case for re-examining what is essentially a good thing is very weak, especially when capital gains taxes remain a significant source of revenue in a difficult year.  There are two parallel areas of reasoning to note here. One relates to the medium-term pressure on the BoP and the rupee in an environment where global interest rates are high and specific sectors like artificial intelligence (AI) are sucking up huge amounts of capital away from emerging markets like India. The other relates to the principles that should govern taxation of incomes arising from capital investments.  Let’s deal with the first issue here — the short- to medium-term pressure on the BoP resulting from outflows of foreign portfolio capital, mainly from the stock markets. Many foreign investors are leaving not because India is a bad story, but because the medium-term prospects for growing their money seem better elsewhere. This outflow, which is being accentuated by the weakness in the rupee despite a massive $140 billion inflow through foreign-currency non-resident (bank) deposits, or FCNR (B), and external borrowings, is worrying the government and the central bank. Administrative measures have been taken by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to prevent excessive speculation and foreign exchange hedging, and oil companies have been given a separate window outside the regular market for foreign exchange purchases. But the weakness continues. The government has also reduced to zero the tax on interest earnings from government securities for foreign investors, which makes sense, for these can be negative-return avenues when the currency is depreciating.  These are good things to do in the short term, but cutting LTCG on equity investments is not just a tactical move. It has long-term implications for both domestic and foreign investor sentiment, not least because we are now changing the rules for arbitrary reasons. In any case, there is no reason to believe that a cut in or the elimination of LTCG tax will actually bring in more dollars, as some foreign investors could well decide that zero LTCG means they can carry their gains out of India for investment in US Treasuries. More so, when they know that this is being done to ease the pressure on the rupee, and could be reversed later. There is no certainty that a tax cut will bring in the dollars rather than prompt investors to take their gains and run.  As a country with a large gap between domestic savings and investment, we need foreign capital, but the right way to attract it is not by cutting capital gains taxes. There is no substitute for making India a long-term and safe bet for patient investors who want to build manufacturing or services entities in this country. This has to be done by making it easier for them to invest here, and not just making it easier for them to exit faster. A blow-hot-blow-cold approach to tax policy will hardly reassure them that policies are stable for the long term. If taxes can be cut on a whim, why can’t they be reintroduced on a whim too?  This brings us to the principles that should underlie taxation of incomes on invested capital. Capital investments generate three basic types of incomes for the investor — interest, dividends, and capital gains. The Modi government has tried to bring dividends on a par with income earned from labour by abandoning the old dividend distribution tax (DDT), which was essentially payable at the corporate end and did not differentiate between dividends paid to a small shareholder and those with large holdings. Essentially, it indirectly taxed small shareholders and benefited large shareholders, including promoters. In parallel, the Modi government raised taxes on earnings from investments in debt to bring them on a par with bank deposits, while also abandoning the tax-free bonds scheme, which again was a benefit only for those in the highest tax brackets.  LTCG rates were raised in the 2024 Budget, and most capital gains on multiple assets were taxed at 12.5 per cent, plus surcharge, where applicable, for higher income earners. Put simply, taxes on dividends were treated on a par with income earned from other sources, while taxes on equity capital gains were treated preferentially. This makes sense to some extent, as equity is risk capital, and India needs risk capital to boost productivity and growth.  One can see the thought behind various changes. The government has been slowly equalising taxes on income from debt and income from salaries and other forms of labour, while keeping taxes on capital gains on favourable terms. Keeping LTCG at a relatively low level compared to taxes on interest, dividends, and income from labour work is probably justified in order to attract risk capital, but zero tax on capital gains? Is there any better way to silently send the message that capital needs to be mollycoddled more than labour, when we have millions needing jobs?  A cut in LTCG can be done in two ways: One, by restricting it to foreign investors, or, two, by making it available to all investors. I don’t think the domestic investor is demanding any such sops for herself, when systematic investment plans are drawing such huge inflows. Why should the government pander only to foreign investors, who are here only for the profits and nothing more? There is a case for not discriminating against hot flows, but certainly not for discriminating against locals to favour foreign investors. An exception can perhaps be made for debt investments, where the rupee’s weakness can deter foreign investors, but not domestic ones.  The principle of taxing incomes should be the same whether one earns it from labour or capital investment. The case for a reasonable differential between taxation of risk capital and labour is probably well-established, but not for a lopsided preference for treating equity with kid gloves.  A strong case for abolishing LTCG tax can be made only when the country decides to abolish income taxes altogether or offers very high tax-free thresholds. For what we are really taxing here is income. Where that income comes from does not matter all that much. And if a cut in LTCG is being considered as a short-term tactical move, like the FCNR (B) gambit, why not say that only equity investments made between now and March 31, 2027, will qualify for these zero rates? But even that is not a good idea, for it complicates the tax regime further — which is not a worthwhile move when we are trying to simplify things. So, no, don’t mess with LTCG.

entry.title: How India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voice
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / How India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voiceHow India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voice

From the intimidating bank manager to the trusted Bhabhi, finance has found a new face

premium

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:39 PM ISTFor 40 years, finance in India had a face. It was a man, 48 years old. In a suit. With a moustache. And glasses that said, “I know more than you.” He sat behind a big wooden desk at a public-sector bank. He spoke in English that you didn’t fully understand. He made you feel small. He made you feel like you had come to ask for a favour, even if it was your own money.  That was finance. Father-like. Strict. Distant. “Beta, form bhar ke laao. Kal aana.” Then, quietly, finance got a sex change. Finance is no longer your father. Finance is now your Bhabhi. And that is the biggest marketing shift in BFSI (Banking, Financial Services and Insurance) in the last decade.  Open any finance ad today. Who is talking? It’s not the suit-man. It’s a warm, smiling, 32-year-old woman in a salwar suit, or a saree, who says, “Arre, SIP toh main bhi karti hoon. Bohot easy hai. Chalo main samjhati hoon.” That’s Bhabhi.  She is not your mother — mothers are too emotional. She is not your wife — wives are too direct. She is not your girlfriend — girlfriends are too risky for finance. She is Bhabhi. The perfect Indian balance. She is your elder, so you respect her. She is family, so you trust her. She is approachable, so you can ask her stupid questions. She will not judge you if you don’t know what mutual fund means. And every financial brand in India has hired her.  HDFC Bank — For 20 years, its ads looked like Aditya Puri in a suit. Now? Its last five campaigns have a young woman in the kitchen, explaining that a personal loan is not a big deal. “Aapka ghar, aapka loan.” The Bhabhi who manages the house budget better than the husband.  SBI YONO — The app that your father found intimidating. Who sells it now? Not the manager. A daughter-in-law in an ad, telling her father-in-law, “Papa, YONO pe FD ho jayegi, aapko branch jaane ki zaroorat nahi.” The Bhabhi has reversed the power. She teaches the older man.  ICICI Prudential — All their mutual fund ads are now Bhabhis. Not experts. “Main apne bachche ke liye SIP karti hoon.” It’s not return, it’s responsibility.  Even the bad boys did it.  Cred — Started with Rahul Dravid as Indiranagar ka gunda, Jim Sarbh, all male cool. What happened? No one understood what CRED does. So they brought in Bhabhi. Now their Instagram is full of women creators explaining, “CRED pe rent pay karne se kya hota hai.” The male cool didn’t convert. The Bhabhi explanation did.  Zerodha — Nithin Kamath is the coolest finance bro in India. But who is actually bringing in Tier 2 women investors? His videos with his wife Seema Patil, and creators like Shreya Kapoor, and Neha Nagar. The language changed from “bullish-bearish” to “dekho, ye stock aise samjho jaise sabzi mandi.”  Why did this happen? Because men ruined finance. For 30 years, we made finance about fear and ego. “You don’t know. I know. So listen to me.” The result? We created a country that saves in gold, under the mattress because gold doesn’t ask for a PAN card.  Finance had a trust deficit, not a knowledge deficit. And trust, in Indian families, doesn’t come from father. It comes from Bhabhi. In every Indian home, who do you go to if you need ₹10,000 urgently without telling anyone? Bhabhi. Who knows your real salary, your real debt, your real gold? Bhabhi.  Who explains your father’s complicated medical report in simple language? Bhabhi. So, finance did the smartest thing. It fired the suited man and hired the Bhabhi.  This is not just about ads. It’s a product strategy.  > SIP is a Bhabhi product. Small, monthly, no big risk, like a kitty. ₹500 per month. Father would have said, “₹5 lakh ka lump sum lao.” Bhabhi says, “₹500 se shuru karte hain.”  > Gold loans are now Bhabhi-fied. Muthoot’s old ads were tough Malayali men with moustaches. Now Manappuram’s ads have Madhuri Dixit saying, “Gold is yours, loan is easy.” She is India’s most loved Bhabhi.  > Insurance is Bhabhi-fied too. LIC’s old ads were about death. HDFC Life’s ads are about “Sar Utha Ke Jiyo” — but explained by a wife to her husband.  The language has changed too. From “wealth creation, portfolio diversification, asset allocation” to “bachche ka future, thoda thoda, chalo saath mein dekhte hain.”  From English to Hindi to Hinglish. From return to responsibility. From fear to care.  Namaste Bhabhi!

entry.title: Amid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK Shivakumar
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Amid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK ShivakumarAmid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK Shivakumar

The strongest Congress government in Karnataka in 37 years looks to be its weakest

premium

Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe Congress won 178 seats of the 224 in the Karnataka Assembly elections in 1989, exactly when the party lost power at the Centre after its stupendous victory five years earlier. And the Karnataka record is unbeaten till today. Veerendra Patil was credited with that victory and he became chief minister. But following communal riots and Patil’s failing health, Rajiv Gandhi removed him, replacing him with S Bangarappa and later Veerappa Moily. It was Mr Moily who led the Congress into the 1994 Assembly polls and it got just 34 seats.  The short point of this statistical overload is that it takes very little to turn spectacular victories into historic defeats. Many think the current Congress government in Karnataka is headed in that direction again.  In the 2023 Assembly elections, the Congress won 135 seats on its own. It was a handsome victory. The party only needed 113 to form the government. Siddaramaiah became chief minister amid rumours that he had committed himself to handing over power to then deputy chief minister D K Shivakumar in 30 months.  That “agreement” had to be enforced by the high command. M Siddaramaiah stepped down in bad grace, and gave way to Mr Shivakumar, considered both resourceful and efficient. But that reputation has unravelled sooner than expected. Today, the strongest Congress government in Karnataka in 37 years looks to be its weakest.  To be fair, not all of the blame should fall on Mr Shivakumar. When the state-run milk cooperative brand Nandini increased milk prices by ₹8 a litre a few days ago (prices of butter and ghee going up was inevitable), it was only following other milk cooperatives across the country. The chief minister pleaded with the cooperative to reduce the increase in curd prices, which it did. But this might have been a tactical mistake. It suggested he had the power to intervene in pricing but was choosing to limit it to curd.  Objective financial reasons also led to the announcement of a 23-35 per cent increase in state-run bus fares last week. Transport Minister Byrathi Suresh told the Legislative Council in September that the four state-owned road transport corporations (RTCs) had posted an annual loss of ₹8,000 crore because of four consecutive increases in the prices of diesel and other petroleum products by the Centre. But women travel on these buses free as part of the Congress’ 2023 poll promise (the Shakti scheme). So, in popular perception, men have been cross-subsidising the fares of the women all along and at the end of the day, the government is recovering its money via a fare elevation so it’s done no one any favours by enabling women to travel free. In fact, the state government reimburses the state transport corporations for the losses incurred by the Shakti scheme. That the state transport corporations are inefficient and corrupt is another story. But in politics, explaining niceties isn’t always easy.  When you add to that the outcome of a sting operation on Siddaramaiah, the current chief minister’s stock falls further. A Congress activist, Kripa Alva, claimed to have a clip showing Siddaramaiah engaged in crimes against minors. The chief minister ordered an enquiry and Ms Alva was expelled from the party but not before Opposition leader H D Kumaraswamy, also a Union minister, alleged that the video clip was released at the behest of the chief minister, whose reputation as the “King of Stings” has spread far and wide. Mr Kumaraswamy’s message is: The Congress is at war with itself. There seems to be no counteroffensive from the state unit of the party. On the contrary, state party chief, B K Hariprasad, has said he is doubtful how fair the enquiry will be since political leaders are involved.   All this is telling on Mr Shivakumar’s famed management skills. The Congress lost all four seats in the recent Legislative Council polls. It isn’t that he doesn’t have efficient colleagues. The minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, is both hardworking and result-oriented. Health Minister U T Khader is known for his calmness and delivery though he became a minister only in June. As minister for industries and infrastructure development, M B Patil is the man behind investment in Karnataka. But political and resource management is ultimately Mr Shivakumar’s responsibility.  The only consolation for the party is that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) seems to be in a lethargic slump. State chief B Y Vijayendra’s term ends on November 10, and despite the party’s performance in the Council elections, his detractors in the party believe he might be between jobs. There seems to be little effort to hit the streets: The BJP’s wars against the government are being fought on social media.  It might be time for Mr Shivakumar to stop, take a deep breath and re-centre himself and his government. Assembly elections are due in the summer of 2028. If he has to pull a rabbit out of a hat, the time is now.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: CR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and records
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / CR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and recordsCR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and records

Fans will long squabble over whether Messi or Ronaldo is entitled to the 'greatest of all time' accolade... this is a pointless exercise

premium

Cristiano Ronaldo

Kanika Datta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:19 PM ISTIn 2003, Manchester United, which lorded over the English Premier League with eight titles and one Champions’ League trophy till then under Alex Ferguson’s forceful stewardship, played a friendly match against Portuguese club Sporting CP. They lost 3-1, but it was the post-match developments that proved decisive for an 18-year-old Cristiano Ronaldo.  He wasn’t on the scoresheet that day, but his dribbling skills and ability to read the game had already caught Sir Alex’s eye. It was the senior Man U players who clinched the decision for him.  On the bus and plane ride home, they badgered their manager — no mean feat given his legendary temper — to sign the teenager. They were pushing at an open door; with the team’s celebrated no. 7, David Beckham, headed for Real Madrid, Man U needed a comparable replacement fast.  Even before he proved himself on the pitch, Ronaldo, sporting a kooky hairstyle and ear studs, made headlines, with Man U paying Sporting CP £12.4 million, a record-breaking sum at the time. Rivals Liverpool and Arsenal, also in the race, dropped out, saying they valued the player at about a quarter that sum. The rest was not just history for Man U — which went on to win three more Premier League titles and one Champions League trophy with him — but for Ronaldo, too. He bagged the first of his five Ballon d’Or awards before going on to a stellar career in Real Madrid and Juventus. He drew a slavish fan following, not just from the teams he represented but neutral and opposition fans as well. Who will forget how the entire stadium stood up to applaud his bicycle kick goal in the 2018 Champions League match against Juventus?    Now, as he hangs up his studs from international football at the ripe age of 41, older heads will judge his retirement as long overdue. Indeed, younger fans who never had the privilege of watching CR7, as his fans called him, in his prime would have wondered what the fuss was all about had they watched his dismal performance in the recent World Cup. Where his great rival Lionel Messi walked and jinked around opposition defenders for Argentina, Ronaldo was a shadow of himself, unable to execute those incredible jumps that earned him the record for the most headed goals in football history (158) or make those darting runs into the box to score the 985 goals of his career. Yet just 10 years before, he powered Portugal to a Uefa Euro trophy, the nation’s first major tournament title, with three goals (all critical ones) and two assists. In the final against France, he was forced off  with knee injury after a cynical tackle. But in a show of inspired captaincy he ran up and down the sidelines — which his manager, marooned in a mandatory technical area, could not do — bellowing instructions and encouragement to his team until a little-known substitute called Eder drove in a goal from a distance to win Portugal the match.    Retiring from international football within a month of each other, fans will long squabble over whether Messi or Ronaldo are entitled the “Greatest of All Time” (GOAT) accolade. As with the Roger Federer versus Rafael Nadal debate in tennis, this is a pointless exercise. One scored more goals (Ronaldo: 985; Messi: 937). The other had more assists (Messi: 428; Ronaldo: 261). One had more Ballon D’Ors (Messi: eight; Ronaldo: five) … and so on and so forth. But as with Federer and Nadal, to reduce Messi and Ronaldo’s careers to stats is to do them a disservice. Both gave fans hours of sheer delight and both contributed to the development of football as we know it in unique ways.  Much has been written about how Messi, who retired on October 6 at age 39, conserved his energy by walking between 40 and 60 per cent per match. Ronaldo represented the new age of iron discipline and fitness that is demanded of top level footballers. Where Diego Maradona, drank and drugged his way through a dazzling career at the age of 33 (though it was over long before that), Ronaldo ate and drank with the fastidiousness of a fashion model. As Sir Alex admiringly wrote in his book Leading, as Ronaldo aged, he kept himself underweight in the interests of agility and speed. Though he would occasionally be photographed with his arm around a “young lady” (Sir Alex’s  words) in a night club, he drank only water and slept early.  If there was a difference between the two greats, it was in their lifestyles. Where Messi has a burnished reputation as a family man ever faithful to his childhood sweetheart, Ronaldo has been dogged by allegations of rape; his attempts to pay for the victim’s silence did not enhance his personal standing. The latter’s contract with the shady Saudi club Al Nassr, which includes influencer fees quite apart from how he performs on the pitch, and a Nike sponsorship deal ensures that he will out-earn Messi by several millions. That, too, is a feature of modern football superstardom. This generation of emerging greats will stand on their shoulders.

entry.title: Making outsourcing work
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Making outsourcing workMaking outsourcing work

Outsourcing strengthens banking only when risks are managed effectively

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Swaminathan J5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 12:16 AM ISTA customer withdrawing cash through a business correspondent, applying for a loan on a fintech platform, or using a banking app supported by an external technology provider may not notice the third party behind the service. Nor should the customer have to. The service may be delivered through a partner, but the trust it rests on is placed in the bank.  Outsourcing is hardly new to banking. Banks have long relied on external agencies for card processing, cash handling, customer acquisition and technology support. What is new is the depth and complexity of these relationships. Today, critical technology infrastructure, lead generation, and other customer interfaces, fraud detection systems, and even elements of credit assessment are outsourced to external service providers. Outsourcing has moved from the periphery of banking towards its operational core.  The case for outsourcing: The economic case begins with specialisation. With the proliferation of third-party service providers and fintechs, financial institutions are no longer required to build every technology platform or develop every specialist capability  in-house. A service provider, by serving several financial institutions, can spread investments in infrastructure, security and skilled personnel across a larger customer base. This can lower costs, improve service quality, and give banks access to capabilities that would otherwise be expensive, especially for smaller institutions. Outsourcing can also convert some fixed expenditure into more flexible operating costs, helping banks adjust capacity as demand changes.

Now, to governpremium

Speed matters alongside cost. Experienced service providers can offer proven systems, regular upgrades, and expertise in cloud services, payments, fraud analytics and artificial intelligence. Agile partnerships can shorten time to market, accommodate growth in transaction volumes, and improve the availability of digital services.  In fact, outsourcing can also strengthen resilience, as specialised providers can offer more robust safeguards and redundancy than smaller institutions could afford to maintain on their own, given the high capital and other fixed costs.  In India, business correspondents, by becoming extended arms of bank branches, have helped deliver formal banking services to communities where brick-and-mortar branches may be uneconomical.  Technology partnerships and fintech-led distribution have helped regulated entities reach new customers, simplify onboarding, and deliver services more conveniently. Such arrangements have enabled institutions of different sizes to participate in the expanding digital financial ecosystem.  Outsourcing is thus more than a cost-saving measure; it can support inclusion and innovation at scale.  New dependencies, emerging risks: The strengths of outsourcing can also create vulnerabilities. The challenge, therefore, is to preserve these gains while managing the risks associated with greater external dependence. A service provider may be cost-effective because it serves many institutions on shared infrastructure; a failure of that infrastructure can then disrupt several of them at once. What is efficient for individual entities may, without adequate safeguards, create systemic concentration risks. The global CrowdStrike-related IT outage in July 2024 demonstrated how widespread dependence on an external technology provider can cause disruption across sectors.  Other risks are closer to the customer. Third parties may mishandle confidential data, suffer cyberattacks, rely on poorly controlled subcontractors, or experience financial distress. In customer-facing activities, agents may mis-sell products, use inappropriate recovery practices, or fail to resolve complaints. Cyber criminals may exploit weaker controls at partner interfaces or among outsourced personnel, potentially compromising sensitive customer data.  Artificial intelligence adds another dimension. External models can improve fraud detection and credit analysis, but their workings may be opaque and their outputs difficult to explain. Models can develop or change biases over time. Using external tools to support decisions must not diminish a bank's ability to understand and challenge the resulting judgements. Accountability remains with the bank: A fundamental principle is that banks may outsource activities, but not responsibility or accountability for outcomes. Customers entrust their money and information to banks, not to technology vendors, agents or fintech partners. Contracts can allocate functions and financial liabilities between parties; they cannot displace the bank’s obligations to customers and regulators. The case, therefore, is for responsible outsourcing, not against outsourcing itself. Certain core management and control functions must remain with the bank. More broadly, banks must retain sufficient expertise to evaluate outsourced work, identify weaknesses and intervene. A bank that no longer understands how an essential service operates cannot oversee it effectively. Therefore, building and maintaining in-house capabilities is crucial. From contracts to continuous oversight: Effective oversight goes beyond selecting a reputable provider or negotiating a comprehensive contract. Due diligence, independent assurance, and customer-complaint analysis help reveal how risks evolve throughout the relationship. A consolidated view of critical dependencies can also highlight concentrations that individual vendor reviews may miss. Operational resilience raises another question: Can essential services continue when a provider encounters difficulties? Tested recovery and backup arrangements, viable exit options and access to critical data become particularly important. Where providers serve several banks, concentration risk also acquires a system-wide dimension that individual institutions cannot address alone. The regulatory approach has evolved accordingly. The Reserve Bank’s (RBI’s) 2025 consolidated outsourcing directions address financial services and IT outsourcing, complemented by its 2026 cybersecurity and technology risk framework. Internationally, the Basel Committee's 2025 principles also emphasise managing third-party risks. Both recognise the need for governance that extends beyond contract signing. Recognising growing technology dependence, the RBI has established specialised teams to examine cyber breaches and disseminate lessons through advisories to regulated entities. The effectiveness of these advisories depends on timely remediation of the identified vulnerabilities by regulated entities.  The way forward: Ultimately, success depends not on how much a bank outsources, but on how well it governs those relationships. Outsourcing is essential to a modern, accessible and innovative financial system. Its benefits can be sustained if institutions remain alert to evolving risks, monitor service providers effectively, and retain the capability to act. Most importantly, the work may move outside a regulated entity; accountability does not.

entry.title: India needs focused investment and public infrastructure to lead in AI
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India needs focused investment and public infrastructure to lead in AIIndia needs focused investment and public infrastructure to lead in AI

India's advantage lies not in emulating the US or China, but in creating a blue ocean of its own

premium

India needs to strengthen its domestic AI research and computing capabilities to develop affordable solutions for global markets

Ajay Kumar -5 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:45 PM ISTWith Aadhaar and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), India has shown that it can solve problems at an unprecedented scale and low cost, and build digital infrastructure that the world looks to emulate. The challenge now is to replicate that achievement in AI research by identifying areas where India can lead, building the capabilities to do so, and creating solutions not just for India but for the world.  AI or artificial intelligence research today spans 10 broad areas: Foundation models, which power general-purpose AI and are being made smaller, faster and more efficient; reasoning, which helps AI solve complex problems step by step; AI agents, which can use tools and carry out tasks independently; multimodal AI, which combines text, images, audio, video and an understanding of the physical world; AI safety, which seeks to make systems reliable, understandable and resistant to misuse; robotics, which enables machines to perceive, decide and act in the real world; AI for science, which accelerates discoveries in medicine, materials, climate and mathematics; hardware, which develops specialised chips and energy-efficient computing; data and learning methods, which help AI learn from fewer examples, generate useful training data and keep improving; and governance, which addresses fairness, privacy, transparency and regulation.    The United States and China dominate global AI research, but with different strengths. The US leads in foundation models, reasoning, agents, safety, AI for science and hardware, supported by vast capital, computing power, and global talent. In 2025, private AI investment reached an astounding $285.9 billion. Nvidia and leading laboratories such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind reinforce this advantage.  China leads in robotics and AI research output, and is rapidly closing the gap in models and chips. State support, scale and efficiency underpin its progress. DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen and Moonshot’s Kimi demonstrate that powerful models can be developed at lower cost. Export controls have also accelerated China’s pursuit of chip self-reliance. Multimodal AI and data-learning methods remain fiercely contested, with both countries advancing video generation and compute-efficient training. Europe leads in governance. Its AI Act is first off the block.  India’s position is evolving. It has genuine strengths in language AI, with AI4Bharat, BharatGen, Sarvam AI and Bhashini developing models and datasets across all 22 scheduled languages. These efforts could find markets worldwide, especially in countries where languages like Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and Punjabi are used. Applied AI is also gaining ground. Wadhwani AI has developed tuberculosis screening and cotton pest management capabilities; IIT Ropar’s Annam.AI provides local weather intelligence to farmers; and IIT Kanpur’s Airawat Research Foundation is developing AI-based air-quality systems. Hosting the AI Impact Summit, endorsed by 92 countries through the New Delhi Declaration, has strengthened India’s voice in AI governance. The IndiaAI Mission has mobilised model-development teams in multiple areas and over 45,000 graphics processing units (GPUs). Investments in data centres are growing exponentially. Yet, frontier capabilities remain limited, compute depends on imported chips, and robotics and safety research need strengthening.  India’s digital public infrastructure offers a lesson for AI research: Rather than imitate America’s approach, India should focus on problems where its scale and diversity confer an advantage. First, multilingual, voice-first AI: Open models for underserved languages could make India a global reference point for societies across Africa, South and Southeast Asia. Second, frugal AI. India should develop efficient, affordable models that run on inexpensive devices, even offline, alongside low-power chips for phones, vehicles and farm equipment.  Third, AI as public infrastructure. Health care, agriculture, education and land records offer opportunities to build reliable AI for environments with limited expertise, imperfect data, and strong accountability requirements. Fourth, evaluation and trust. India can develop multilingual benchmarks, test for social biases, detect deepfakes and establish safety standards relevant to the Global South. Achieving this will require substantially deeper research capabilities.  The following six steps may turn these priorities into reality. First, create a dedicated institution. A National AI Development Organisation, structured as a non-govt public entity, with 26 per cent government ownership, 26 per cent held by State Bank of India and Life Insurance Corporation, 30 per cent by the IT industry, and the balance by philanthropic and academic institutions, could provide the focused leadership that National Payments Corporation of India brought to digital payments. It could build critical AI research and deployment infrastructure.  Second, provide ₹25,000 crore -30,000 crore annual funding for a decade concentrated in selected priorities rather than spread thinly. Third, publicly-funded models, datasets and benchmarks should be openly available. The Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture , which enables secure, consent-based AI training should be rolled out on a mission-mode. Formally adopting it could turn AIKosh and Bhashini into trusted data commons for health, agriculture, education and speech. Fourth, make government the first customer. It can create demand and help promising Indian AI solutions scale. Fifth, invest in talent. A thousand research chairs, several thousand doctoral fellowships modelled on the Vishveshwariah PhD scheme of 2014, and efforts to attract Indian researchers abroad could strengthen research capacity.  Sixth, expand computing and chip design. Scale shared GPU access, fund national supercomputing, and support energy-efficient AI chips through Semicon India, combining design grants, fabrication access and assured government purchases.  India must not repeat its semiconductor experience in AI. Indian talent designed world-class chips, but the intellectual property (IP) belonged largely to global majors. India must urgently create and scale its own IP, for India and the world. India should not race to build AI that merely matches the world’s best. That is a red ocean, crowded with giants. Its opportunity lies in a blue ocean of its own: AI that speaks every language and runs on the billions of devices in people’s hands.

entry.title: Landlord's dividend: The opportunity of financing India's data centres
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Landlord's dividend: The opportunity of financing India's data centresLandlord's dividend: The opportunity of financing India's data centres

Data centres offer banks and insurers an opportunity for long-term lending, but financing AI chips carries higher risks

premium

A data centre with rows of servers, reflecting India's growing focus on AI infrastructure and digital computing (Photo: Shutterstock)

Dipak Gupta8 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:25 PM ISTCan you think of an infrastructure investment that pays for itself in under a year? Or, if you believe some people, in six month.  Most of us who have lent to roads and power plants would say no. A toll road takes 15 years or more to earn back its cost, and a power plant around the same. Yet that is now being said about artificial intelligence (AI) compute in America. Jensen Huang says he has heard of investments returning their capital inside 12 months. Elon Musk thinks six months next year is “not impossible”. Nebius put the payback on its larger recent deals at a year and 10 months.  Returns like these go to whoever owns the chips, and in India that is mostly not us. But a good part of the boom is being built here, and I find it useful to think of it in two layers. The first is the data centre itself: Land, building, substations, cooling, water, the generator sets in the yard. The second is what goes inside it, the chips. Indian banks can finance the first without breaking a sweat. The second needs a lot more thought.  India, the landlord  India’s boom is much smaller, and of a different kind. Operational capacity should touch about 2 gigawatt (Gw) by December, and most forecasts for 2030 sit between 5 and 8 Gw. The announcements are higher. Adani 5 Gw by 2035, AirTrunk 5 GW by 2030, Google 1 Gw at Vizag, a multi-Gw Reliance campus at Jamnagar. Interestingly, commitments since 2021 add up to about $175 billion. US’ four largest hyperscalers will spend nearly four times that amount this year alone.  Most of what we are building is real estate with a very large electricity bill. Apart from Reliance and Yotta, Indian money is going into land, power and buildings, rented to Google, Microsoft and Amazon, who bring their own chips. NTT’s Indian business earns about ₹9.7 crore of revenue per megawatt (Mw), and assuming a 40 per cent margin a new building needs something like 15 years to repay itself. No equity investor gets excited by that. A project lender should.  Two layers, two very different loans  The building, with its power and cooling, costs ₹50-70 crore per Mw, or $5-7 million, depending on whose estimate you prefer. The chips cost several times as much. By Jensen Huang’s own reckoning, Nvidia’s share of a Gw is about $25 billion for Blackwell and $40 billion for the coming Rubin generation: $25–40 million per Mw, counting only what Nvidia sells. The building will last 25 years. The chips run the risk of looking dated in a few years.  Layer one: The building  Taking India from 2 Gw to 5-10 Gw means building another 3-8 Gw. At ₹60-70 crore a Mw, that is ₹2-5 trillion by 2030, before anyone builds the power plants to run them. If 60-70 per cent is debt, banks are looking at ₹1.2-3.5 trillion of fresh lending. Put that next to what banks already hold. Bank credit to all of Indian infrastructure was ₹15.1 trillion in June 2026. The buildings alone could add 8-23 per cent to that book in four years, somewhere between a fifth and more than half of what banks now add to infrastructure lending each year. The solar farms and transmission lines behind them come on top.  This is lending our banks understand, and the credit is better than a fair bit of what they already carry. A toll road lives on traffic forecasts, and a power plant on the goodwill of a state discom. A data centre’s tenant is Microsoft or Google, often signed up before the building is finished, in a market where JLL puts vacancy at a record low of 2.8 per cent. Some banks are already at it: SBI and Central Bank have lent ₹5,500 crore to CtrlS, and eight global banks up to $1.44 billion to AdaniConneX. Insurers have a part to play too. A recent tax change makes sale-and-leasebacks and data-centre InvITs possible, so a bank can build, sell the finished asset to an insurer or a pension fund, and move on to the next campus.  Layer two: The chips  The second layer is where the real money is, but also the real risk. Most chips that come to India will sit on Microsoft’s or Google’s balance sheet and never come near an Indian banker. What is open to us is the Indian-owned slice. Reliance is building several gigawatts at Jamnagar, and Yotta wants to grow from 180 Mw to 800 Mw by 2029. If even one Gw of India’s build-out is filled with chips owned by Indian companies, that is $25-40 billion, or ₹2.4–3.8 trillion. At two gigawatts, the chips would need more money than all the buildings put together. A chip is seemingly weaker collateral. It is bought in dollars, rented out on contracts of three years or less, and its value in five years depends on whatever Nvidia launches next. Only a few of our largest banks can even attempt this. The Reserve Bank of India caps a bank’s exposure to any one corporate group at 25 per cent of its Tier-I capital, and a single Gw of chips would take even State Bank of India past that limit. In practice it will be a handful of large banks lending together, with alternative investment funds (AIFs) and credit funds alongside.  It will also need clever structuring, and we have plenty now from America. Reading about it took me back to the good old days of sale-and-leaseback and residual-value financing. Meta moved its Hyperion campus into a joint venture 80 per cent owned by Blue Owl funds, which borrowed $27.3 billion against it; Meta leases it back four years at a time and guarantees its residual value should it walk away. CoreWeave borrows against its customer contracts and graphic processing units (GPUs), on five-year loans against three-year contracts, so its lenders are betting on what the chips will fetch later. Its unsecured bonds now are underwater, yielding over 15 per cent.  Closer home, we’ve seen some of this in aircraft leasing, now finding its feet in GIFT City. A GPU is much like a plane, except that it ages in dog years. I would expect chips to be sold to, and leased back from, vehicles owned by banks or AIFs, with loans sized to the customer contract rather than the chip’s hoped-for life and a residual-value guarantee where one can be had. The banks would hold the senior debt. The AIFs would earn their double-digit returns for taking a view on what a used chip is worth.    What could go wrong  For the buildings, power is the hard part, and the problem is the grid more than generation: In the first quarter of 2026 India curtailed 300 gigawatt-hours (Gwh) of renewable power because transmission could not carry it. Each Mw needs 25-30 million litres of water a year, often in cities already short of it. Developers have increased from 5 to 18 since 2019, Icra says rents are already softening, and 12 Gw of announcements against 5-8 Gw of forecast demand in itself has the makings of a glut.  The chips do carry sharper risks — obsolescence, contracts that run out before the loans do, dollar debt against rupee income. A company that borrows to rent out assets that lose value this quickly is, for practical purposes, a non-banking financial company, and we have seen how those behave when the good times end. None of this is a reason to stay away. It is a reason to lend on signed leases and secured power, and to be cautious about residual value.  The landlord’s dividend  America is paying for scarcity, and the money is being made mostly by those who own the chips. We have neither the chips nor the cloud businesses built on them, and I don’t see that changing this decade. It is a little disheartening.  The first layer, though, is ours for the asking. It is a ₹2-5 trillion book of long, contracted lending to some of the best credits in the world. I can think of very few better opportunities for our banks and insurers over the next few years.  The second layer will be for the few large banks and AIFs willing to learn what a used chip is worth. We will not be designing these chips anytime soon. With a bit of old-fashioned financial engineering, we could at least be financing them and hoping to earn the returns provided by short payback periods. 
The writer is a Professor of Practice at IIT Bombay. He retired as MD & CEO of Kotak Mahindra Bank. entry.title: Treat shareholders as shareholders or India may lose compassionate capital
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Treat shareholders as shareholders or India may lose compassionate capitalTreat shareholders as shareholders or India may lose compassionate capital

Tata Trusts dispute must be resolved under company law, without questioning the rights of charitable trusts as shareholders

premium

The Tata Trusts hold about 66 per cent of Tata Sons whose articles give directors nominated by the Trusts an affirmative vote, in effect a consent, on key matters, including the chairman’s appointment

Nitin Potdar6 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:23 PM ISTCommentators framing the Tata Trusts versus Tata Sons saga as a “crisis” for Indian capitalism are entirely beside the point. Critics argue that a “self-perpetuating philanthropic governance structure” operating “without transparency or market discipline” violates the “essential principle of capitalism”. Impressive vocabulary.  However, these objections completely deflect from the real issue, failing a simple, definitive test: The Companies Act, 2013.  Back to first principles  Every company begins with its shareholders. They subscribe to the memorandum, frame the articles and bring the company to life. Section 10 makes the articles a binding contract between the company and every member. The articles decide how the board is formed, how business is conducted and which decisions need special approval.  Shareholders appoint directors in a general meeting under Section 152 and can remove them by ordinary resolution under Section 169. The board manages the business, but Section 166 binds every director to act in accordance with the articles. Directors have duties.  Shareholders have authority. Directors run the company; shareholders decide the constitution it runs under, and who runs it. The Act does not grade its shareholders. A promoter, a private equity (PE) fund, a multinational parent or the trustees of a public charitable trust hold the same share with the same rights. Section 47 gives every equity shareholder a vote in proportion to paid-up capital. The Act never asks who the shareholder is, where the money came from, or what will be done with the dividend.  The real question  The Tata Trusts hold about 66 per cent of Tata Sons whose articles give directors nominated by the Trusts an affirmative vote, in effect a consent, on key matters, including the chairman’s appointment. The Supreme Court upheld those articles in 2021 as legally valid. On September 17, the board reappointed N Chandrasekaran with the two Trust nominees divided and a casting vote deciding the matter. The Trusts said the articles were not honoured.  That is the core issue, and it is narrow: Did the resolution satisfy Article 121? It is a question of reading a contract and, if need be, one for the courts. It is not answered by asking whether a charity should own what it has owned for a century. The jargon does not illuminate that question. It changes the subject.  Fanciful questions, settled law  The Act does not make voting rights dependent on whether a shareholder can be bought out on a stock exchange. It does not ask a shareholder to prove skin in the game, or to explain how its own governing body is chosen. A PE fund’s investment committee is not elected by the public. A family holding company’s board is not chosen through an open process, even when family feuds tear a business apart. No one asks them to justify their vote at a general meeting, and the Act gives no one that right.  On risk, the Trusts bear more than any shareholder on the register. They cannot sell, cannot diversify and have no other endowment. They have historically taken only a small share of Tata Sons’ dividends, leaving the rest to compound in the business.  On discipline, trustees answer to the Charity Commissioner under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950, who can audit them, inquire into their conduct, surcharge them for loss and remove them. A trustee holds shares only for the trust’s purpose. To use them for himself would be a breach of trust. No fund manager or promoter faces that much scrutiny.  Nor is an affirmative vote exotic. In joint ventures (JVs) and PE deals, I have rarely seen a significant investment without a long list of reserved matters. Multinational corporations (MNCs) insist on them; funds will not invest without them. Nobody calls them undemocratic then.  Disclosure, not dispossession  Fairness demands one concession, and only one. How trustees are chosen and how conflicts are handled are part of the trust’s design; that was the settlors’ wish. Rewriting that design is like rewriting a will after the testator has gone, with no one left to defend his intent. The Trusts can fairly be asked to disclose more. But the rights of the shareholder are a different matter. They flow from the shares and the articles, exactly as they do for everyone else. To confuse the two is dispossession dressed up as reform.  If a shareholder’s rights can be argued away because of who that shareholder is, no shareholder is safe. Today it is a charity. Tomorrow it could be a promoter family, a foreign investor or a fund. The sanctity of the articles is not a Tata issue. It is India’s.  The real cost  The deeper harm is to compassionate capital. Sir Ratan Tata and Sir Dorabji Tata could have left their shares to their families. Instead, they gave them to strangers they would never meet and tied them permanently to a public purpose. That is trust by design. A century later, those shares fund hospitals, cancer care, scholarships and research, while the profits left in the business built the group.  India is creating wealth faster than at any time in its history. Its new founders will ask one question before they give: If I place my shares in a trust for the public good, will the  law respect that trust as a shareholder, or will commentators argue its rights away at the first dispute? If the answer is uncertain, they will keep their shares in the family.  Indian philanthropy will remain a matter of cheques, never of ownership.  Denmark, Germany and Switzerland settled this long ago. Novo Nordisk, Carlsberg, Bosch and Rolex are controlled by foundations, and their governments protect the model rather than question it.  Let the Tata dispute be settled the way company law settles every dispute: By the articles, the board and, if need be, the courts. But let no one suggest that a shareholder deserves fewer rights because it chose to serve the public rather than itself. The Companies Act draws no such distinction. Neither should we.
The writer is a senior corporate and M&A lawyer     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Tata Trusts Tata Sons shareholder Tata group

entry.title: The macro-micro Nobel in economics
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The macro-micro Nobel in economicsThe macro-micro Nobel in economics

A very consequential award for economic policy and people's lives

premium

The Nobel Prize in Economics recognises work by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford that connected microeconomic behaviour with macroeconomic stabilisation, offering insights into how monetary and fiscal policies shape economies and people's lives.| Ilu

Ajay Chhibber6 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 11:41 PM ISTWhen I landed in Palo Alto, California, in September 1978 to start a PhD programme at Stanford University, there was a buzz about Robert Hall’s paper in the Journal of Political Economy on the Life-Cycle Permanent Income Hypothesis.1  Bob, as he was called, was a dashing young Stanford professor with a sports car bearing TSP on its number plate, named for the Time Series Processor computer program he created when he was a graduate student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Along with Michael Woodford of Columbia University, he was awarded the Nobel Prize for economics this year for the body of work they started called the micro foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.  Bob’s paper showed consumption depended not on current income but on expected permanent income, and , therefore, only unexpected and permanent changes in policy could affect the path of consumption and employment. This fundamental insight was central to the New Keynesian models developed thereafter. In 1978, the world was still recovering from the 1973-74 oil shock, which had created a new phenomenon called stagflation — high inflation coexisting with high unemployment. Existing models could not explain stagflation, as prices and wages were assumed to adjust to equilibrate markets and remove unemployment. Subsequently a bevy of economists — Guillermo Calvo, Stanley Fischer, Michael Bruno, Olivier Blanchard, Ben Bernanke (Nobel Prize winner, who also taught me macroeconomics at Stanford in 1980), Joseph Stiglitz and George Akerlof — developed models that introduced wage and price rigidities, information asymmetries and credit market imperfections to explain stagflation and brought back a role for fiscal policy, which monetarists like Milton Friedman and Edward C Prescott (both Nobel winners) had earlier dismissed as inconsequential for smoothing consumption.  Michael Woodford synthesised all this work in his now famous book Interest and Prices, where he presented the basic structure of the New Keynesian macroeconomics built using microeconomic insights into consumer and firm behaviour on how price expectations are formed, prices and wages are set, and how central bankers and tax policy can influence that behaviour. John Taylor, also at Stanford, could have been added to the Prize as his famous Taylor rule is also central to the New Keynesian framework synthesised by Dr Woodford.  The insights from the New Keynesian framework have been hugely influential. Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke used it after the 2008 financial crisis to help the United States recover, although, in my humble opinion, he may have gone too far with quantitative easing (QE), whereby the central bank starts buying financial assets once policy interest rates have dropped to near zero. His third and fourth waves of QE had marginal benefits.  It has again been extremely helpful more recently in Fed Chair Jerome Powell’s handling of the recovery from the Covid pandemic, when he was accused initially of misdiagnosing inflation as temporary but subsequently managed to contain inflation without causing a recession. Donald Trump’s tariffs and misguided war in Iran have stoked inflation and not allowed Mr Powell to finish the job. His successor Kevin Warsh has inexplicably dropped forward guidance from his tool kit and may have made his job harder.  I was fortunate to interact with some of the contributors to this edifice. I worked closely with Stanley Fischer when he was chief economist at the World Bank, and we co-edited a pioneering book on African economics. Michael Bruno, another chief economist, asked me to lead the seminal World Development Report 1997 on the role of the state, which emphasised the importance of an effective state and regulation. After he passed away unexpectedly, we finished that Report under the next chief economist, Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz.  But these great minds did not always agree. Stanley Fischer went on to hold key positions at the International Monetary Fund, but surprisingly initially supported harsh fiscal policy, which exacerbated the Asian Financial Crisis, something quite contrary to what the New Keynesian framework would have suggested. Joe Stiglitz was a harsh critic of those policies and of premature liberalisation of capital accounts, which had created the Asian financial crisis.  New Keynesian frameworks have, no doubt, helped design better stabilisation policies in the developed world, as the Nobel committee suggests. But these policies have also had huge spillovers, which make macro-management in developing countries more difficult, both when the stimulus is introduced and when it is withdrawn. Money flows in, making exchange rate management and monetary policy more complicated, and the reverse happens when money suddenly flows out. But that does not in any way detract from the magnificent work done by our two current Nobel Prize winners and the spillovers must, in any case, be dealt with separately.  The New Keynesian framework was not helpful in a developing country’s context because the information and financial depth needed for a permanent income hypothesis to be relevant do not exist. Unlike in the developed world, a very sizeable percentage live hand-to-mouth, so traditional Keynesian approach to stimulate demand works. In addition, with large informal markets and generalised under-employment, the concept of an output gap — the difference between actual and potential output — central to the New Keynesian framework is not valid for a developing country. Nevertheless, some studies have found the New Keynesian models with forward expectations and an output gap valid and others have not.  In my own recent work on India’s inflation, I did not find the output gap helpful. But I also find the structural school of inflation, which ignores monetary policy and expectations, incomplete, as it cannot explain what generates broader inflation. Instead, I find that a variable mark-up pricing (not Michael Bruno’s fixed mark-up model) with a hybrid monetarist-structural approach2 fits well with India’s reality. As India’s economy develops, becomes more formal and gains financial depth, tools developed by the New Keynesian framework may become more relevant.  Meanwhile, going back to the Nobel Prize I am so happy that a micro-macro approach to understanding how economies behave has been recognised. Macroeconomists and microeconomists typically do not talk to each other, but here is evidence of why they should. Dr Hall was famous for saying, “Macroeconomics is just applied microeconomics.” This year’s Nobel winners — Hall and Woodford — follow theoretical insights with hard-core empirical work. No armchair theorising here, but consequential frameworks that improve policies and people’s lives. 
 The writer is distinguished visiting scholar, Institute for International Economic Policy, George Washington University 1. Stochastic-JPE-Dec-1978.pdf 2. A Variable Mark-up Model of Inflation in India   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
