entry.title: Green crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impact
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Green crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impactGreen crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impact

Green crackers and restricted timings may do little to ease pollution in the National Capital Region

premium

A child lights a firecracker during Diwali celebrations (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:42 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has negotiated the thin line between popular sentiment and public health and environmental concerns by extending conditional permission for bursting green crackers within a restricted time window on November 7 and 8. At a time when the air-quality index swings between “severe” and “hazardous”, this well-meaning order is unlikely to clear the air around or after Diwali. For one, enforcing these restrictions demands a level of monitoring that is well beyond the capabilities or the inclination of the state police forces or the political administration. Two years ago, the apex court sharply rebuked the Delhi Police for its inability to enforce the cracker ban. It is also doubtful whether the restrictions limiting firecracker sales to products certified by government bodies can be monitored, let alone implemented. Media reports have already tracked hectic clandestine sales of non-green fireworks, which a certain kind of consumer demands because they literally offer more bang for the buck than the green variants do — and are available in elusive popup shops in small lanes. Fake QR codes have also proliferated.     But the genuine health and environmental safety of green crackers themselves remains doubtful. The Supreme Court has stipulated that only crackers certified by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-Neeri) or the Petroleum and Safety Organisation (Peso) and identified with specific QR codes can be sold. Though both CSIR-Neeri and Peso are guaranteed to follow strict standards, the problem lies in the definition of “green cracker”, which may be somewhat misleading. They are said to reduce particulate matter (PM) 2.5 and 10 by some 30 per cent and emit 10 per cent less harmful gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide. They also exclude toxic chemicals such as barium nitrate, lithium and cadmium found in traditional crackers. But they still emit smoke and PM, and are only marginally less harmful than traditional crackers. The apex court has, perhaps, overlooked the sheer volume of crackers that are burnt over the course of Dussehra and Diwali. Last year, a survey showed that the number of families bursting fire crackers rose 40 per cent over the previous year and half of them intended to burn traditional firecrackers alongside green ones. Even assuming that all consumers in the National Capital Region (NCR) are stricken by conscience and choose to burn only green firecrackers within the specified timings, the emission of PM10 and PM2.5 will still be high enough to create the characteristic post-Diwali haze compounded by unabated seasonal farm fires and low wind speeds.  It is possible that the Supreme Court has chosen a realistic path, given the cussedness of citizens who decline to cut back firecracker burning in the broader public interest. Since the popular discourse often centres on the right to freely practise religion, the court has stated that this right is not absolute. The court has balanced this right by invoking Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty, which the judges have interpreted as the right to a healthy, safe, and pollution-free environment. Outright bans have been spectacularly unsuccessful, so this via-media approach may assuage public and politico-religious sentiment. Even assuming the court’s diktat is followed, the burning of green crackers, which are, in fact, not so green, is unlikely to offer the NCR’s citizens a happy, pollution-free Diwali.   Topics : Supreme Court Diwali pollution Firecrackers Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: RBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / RBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictionsRBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictions

The evolving global economic and financial conditions have resulted in significant volatility in the Indian financial market

premium

Reserve Bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:40 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) this week constituted a technical consultative committee for financial markets. It is expected to facilitate structured engagement with market participants and stakeholders on policy and operational issues relating to money markets, government securities, foreign-exchange markets, derivatives markets, and infrastructure. The committee, with most members drawn from outside the central bank, should help enable more informed intervention. Any such committee of experts that provides a forum for discussion involving market participants with the objective of improving the functioning of financial markets must be welcomed, particularly against the given backdrop.  The evolving global economic and financial conditions have resulted in significant volatility in the Indian financial market. While equity and bond markets have witnessed volatility over the past several months, the RBI’s focus has largely been on the currency markets. Although the rupee has gained over the past few trading sessions, it has been under considerable pressure, at least since the beginning of the Iran war. India faced the prospect of an increased current-account deficit along with persistent outflows on the capital account. The RBI also announced swap schemes to attract foreign flows and build buffers. It has used foreign-exchange reserves to stem the decline in the rupee. India’s foreign-exchange reserves have declined by about $66 billion from the record highs of $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4. It has also put various restrictions in the market for currency derivatives with a view to containing speculation.  It is in this context that the committee will have consultation with stakeholders. It is hoped that its deliberations and consequent RBI intervention will be made public for wider discussion. Notably, one of the terms of reference for the committee is: “Emerging policy and operational issues affecting financial markets, including implementation of RBI measures and identification of unintended market frictions.” This is a crucial aspect, and it would be interesting to know the views of the committee. One of the issues has been the level of central-bank intervention. As one of the experts pointed out on these pages recently, in 2025-26, the RBI bought government bonds worth about 2.5 per cent of gross domestic product, which was over 80 per cent of net central-government borrowing. This partly compressed government bond yields and reduced the yield difference with other markets, and may have affected capital flows. The RBI intervention was to improve liquidity, which got drained owing to foreign-exchange outflows and intervention in that market. More recently, the RBI was busy draining liquidity out of the market. Liquidity increased substantially with large inflows under the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits. The data shows that the RBI also had a net short dollar position worth about $240 billion in the forward market at the end of September. Clearly, it is trying to manage various things in the market.   It must be accepted that spillovers from global markets often complicate things in emerging-market economies. However, it must also be recognised that as India gets more integrated with the global economy, partly owing to new free-trade agreements, it will become increasingly difficult for the RBI to influence market outcomes without creating friction. For instance, last financial year, India exported goods and services worth over $850 billion, while imports stood above $950 billion. Thus, nearly about $2 trillion crossed the Indian borders in a year on just the trade account. Therefore, the need is to develop markets, not restrict them, and allow economic agents to take informed business decisions. The expert committee should be expected to draw up a fresh road map.   Topics : RBI Financial markets Foreign exchange reserves

entry.title: Now, to govern
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Now, to governNow, to govern

Democrats must build credible policies

premium

The Democrats’ gains in the US midterm elections have delivered a strong rebuke to President Donald Trump’s policies, but the party now faces the challenge of turning electoral success into credible governance. | Image: Reuters

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 11:42 PM ISTThe blue tsunami in the United States (US) mid-term elections, with the Democrats exceeding expectations by taking control of both chambers of Congress and sweeping the majority of gubernatorial seats, has delivered a decisive rejection of President Donald Trump’s policies. The Democrats flipped several governor, House of Representatives, and Senate races, unseating veteran incumbents and decades-old Republican strangleholds. They also placed, for the first time, a Latina as Texas governor and a Muslim in the Senate. Mr Trump repudiated responsibility for his party’s poor showing, saying he wasn’t on the ballot although, before the polls, he had told the electorate to vote as though he were on the ballot. But Democrat euphoria needs to be tempered by the sobering reality of governance.  Despite the headline-grabbing donations from Big Tech — notably Elon Musk — for the Republicans, the Democrats benefited from an outsize electoral budget, outspending its rival by $800 million, according to OpenSecrets, a non-partisan authority on spending in US elections. A record turnout of African Americans and young people, traditional Democrat voters, also helped. But at the heart of this verdict has been the citizenry’s dissatisfaction with the rising cost of living, which is a result of high tariff walls, and the Iran war, which sent gasoline prices soaring. The Democrats will be fully tested on this account. Broadly, they propose a mix of price controls for consumer products, rent freezes, enhanced subsidies for health care and housing, enforcing a clean-energy transition, and tariff rollbacks. Apart from restoring Medicare, the efficacy of the other policies is open to question.  The soaring debt of the US government leaves little space for affordable house-building programmes and subsidies. The Nixon-era imposition of price controls in 1971 to counter inflation proved a long-term failure with large-scale shortages and a huge rebound in prices when the controls were lifted. Tariff reversals, on the other hand, risk alienating traditional Democrat bases of labour unions and small businesses. It is worth noting that Joe Biden as President did not roll back tariffs imposed by Mr Trump in his first term precisely for this reason.  Much, then, depends on ending the war on Iran and re-opening the Strait of Hormuz. Judging from attacks on Iran ahead of the polls, there is little sign that Mr Trump plans to back down. The new Congress will only take power in end-January, which gives the President 60 to 90 days to do things as planned. Although the Republican-controlled Congress, in a remarkable display of bipartisanship, passed a measure demanding the President stop the war against Iran in June under the mostly meaningless War Powers Act, Mr Trump has leveraged his constitutional authority as commander-in-chief to ignore the resolutions. Since Congress also voted him a large budget to continue his Iran policy, he has a funding cushion to continue his Iran campaign. Having ruled through a record number of executive orders in his second term, he is likely to double down on this instrument to further his agenda. Mr Trump has also signalled that he plans to fully leverage his veto powers against Bills passed by the Democrat-controlled Congress. Congress will then require a supermajority to override the presidential veto, no small challenge in the current climate of political polarisation. In short, the next two years of this lame-duck presidency will mark interesting times for the American people — and the world.   Topics : Donald Trump BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment US Election US mid-term elections US Democratic Party Convention

entry.title: Accounting deficiencies
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Accounting deficienciesAccounting deficiencies

Issues raised by the CAG should be addressed

premium

The CAG’s 2025-26 report highlights gaps in government accounting, internal controls and enforcement, underscoring the need to ensure that audit findings translate into actual recoveries and better public administration.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTThe Comptroller and Auditor General of India’s (CAG’s) new report, Adding Value to Public Governance 2025-26, noted that its audits led to recoveries of ₹4,251.34 crore in 2025-26. However, in several major cases, the amount recovered or the corrective action taken fell short of the financial implications flagged by the CAG. At various levels, its findings led to 74 amendments to laws, rules and regulations, 231 changes to government orders and notifications, and 253 revisions to accounting policies and procedures. These figures indicate that audit can influence governance beyond financial recovery. Yet the gap between findings and outcomes remain a concern. In Odisha, for instance, a revenue implication of ₹10,294.24 crore from the undervaluation of iron-ore grades led to a recommendation for an investigation covering all auctioned mines. The reported response was the notification of new mineral rules in 2025, providing for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled surveillance and Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking.  While these measures could improve oversight, the report notes that their impact depends on effective implementation and enforcement. Under a welfare scheme in Odisha, ₹ 782.26 crore was disbursed to 1.27 million ineligible beneficiaries while ₹107.64 crore went to beneficiaries with incorrect bank account details. The reported corrective step was to integrate the scheme’s database with the government schemes and other databases. The case on the oil cess points to a different weakness: Nearly ₹2.9 trillion in cess on crude oil collected by the Union government up to 2023-24 had not been transferred to a designated fund because it had not been created. In response, the Union government subsequently established the Oil Industry Development Fund and transferred ₹17,730 crore, which is about 6 per cent of the amount cited. These examples show that corrective measures and partial transfers do not necessarily resolve the full financial implications identified by audit.  The findings expose several weaknesses. They clearly suggest that internal control and checks are weak at various levels of government. The problem is not only that lapses occur but also that systems often fail to detect them early, prevent their recurrence, or ensure timely corrective action. Besides, audit observations do not automatically translate into public money recovered or better administration. Delays, litigation, weak departmental followups and poor internal controls allow losses to persist. A change in rules or the integration of databases may address the source of an irregularity, but its effectiveness must be judged by measurable outcomes. Stronger legislative scrutiny and fresh audits can help ensure that audit objections are resolved rather than left pending.  The CAG has proposed greater use of technology for identifying risks, anomalies, and weaknesses in internal controls with greater precision and speed. However, technology cannot compensate for weak enforcement or inadequate administrative capacity. Governments need stronger internal audit processes, transparent reporting, and followup audits to verify corrective action and prevent repeat irregularities. This report is a timely reminder that accountability must extend beyond identifying failures to correcting them. The aim should be to collect revenue where it is due, account for it properly, and spend efficiently.   Topics : cag Comptroller and Auditor General CAG BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment CAG audit public funds

entry.title: A trust deficit
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A trust deficitA trust deficit

Govt must respect arbitral awards

premium

The Supreme Court of India, which heard the long-running arbitration dispute involving the government and Vedanta

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has succinctly articulated a key impediment to a vibrant investment climate in India: The Government of India’s consistent refusal to honour arbitral awards. The court was hearing a 22-year-old dispute in which the government was challenging an arbitral award — for a third time — in a production-sharing contract with a consortium to develop oil and gas fields in the Krishna-Godavari basin. The arbitration, which began in 2004, has had a tortuous journey through an arbitration panel award to Vedanta (then Cairn Energy) and Ravva Oil (Singapore) in Kuala Lumpur, unsuccessful appeals in the Malaysian courts, a $99 million demand from the government, a second round of litigation in Malaysia, rejection by the Delhi High Court in 2026, and finally, a Supreme Court appeal. The two-judge Bench of Justice J B Pardiwala and Justice Manmohan pointed to the Centre’s practice of contesting the enforcement of the arbitration award after decades of litigation. They pointed out “no one would trust the government” if it persisted with such practices.  The issue of trust is intrinsic to international commerce. Yet the government’s maximalist legal approach or its penchant for leveraging its policymaking powers to elude contractual arbitration awards has become a sticking point in concluding bilateral investment treaties (BITs) or in India’s emergence as a credible arbitration centre. In 2012, for instance, the Manmohan Singh government passed a law taxing, with retrospective effect, overseas deals involving Indian corporations. The law triggered international arbitration for Vodafone’s acquisition of Hutchison’s share in Hutchison Essar and a corporate reorganisation for Cairn Energy in India, both of which the government lost but declined to honour.  Then followed embarrassing developments as Cairn moved to seize Indian state assets in France and the United Kingdom to enforce the award, after which the retrospective tax law was scrapped in 2021. But the fact that the Narendra Modi government terminated most of the BITs in 2016, including with major trading partners, underlined New Delhi’s inherent intransigence to international arbitration. Since then, the replacement Model BIT introduced a five-year exhaustion clause of local remedies. The policy yielded BITs with a handful of mostly marginal countries. This encouraged the government to soften its approach. The 2024 BITs with the United Arab Emirates is reported to have reduced the local-remedy clause to three years and the one with Saudi Arabia had a two-year stipulation. Trading partners have sought a one-year clause, which New Delhi has not accepted so far.  The government remains an energetic litigator against arbitral awards, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the challenges against those filed before the Delhi High Court between 2021 and 2024, according to a study. The government has admitted in Parliament that state-owned power and road corporations accounted for more than 60 per cent of the challenges. Given this record and the snail-paced functioning of the judicial system, it is no surprise that long-drawn efforts to establish India as a major arbitration hub have gone nowhere, despite legislative amendments to facilitate a faster enforcement of arbitral awards. Investors are likely to weigh these developments against the government’s persistent evasive proclivities. The Cairn-Ravva saga does not enhance confidence in the government as a business partner or predictable policymaker.     Topics : Supreme Court Arbitration International Arbitration Centre Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Fundamental factors
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Fundamental factorsFundamental factors

FPI taxation and capital flows should not be mixed

premium

FPIs this year net sold Indian stocks worth about ₹2.9 trillion and were net sellers in 2025 too

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTDespite the recent pullback in equity markets, considerable anxiety exists among retail investors, including those investing through mutual funds in a disciplined manner using systematic investment plans. The benchmark Nifty 50 is down about 9 per cent since the beginning of this year and is flat since January 2025. Persistent selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) is one reason for this underperformance.  FPIs this year net sold Indian stocks worth about ₹2.9 trillion and were net sellers in 2025 too. This has led to demands that taxes on them should be reconsidered. The argument is that most jurisdictions don’t tax foreign investors, which tends to affect the capital-allocation decisions of large international fund managers.  In this context, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, during an interaction this week, acknowledged the concern over sustained FPI selling. However, the minister rightly pointed out that the tax structure was the same when India received robust capital inflows in 2023-24. No changes had been made to attract capital flows. She did acknowledge that the circumstances had changed since then. It has been reported that the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has also recommended removing long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax imposed on foreign investors. Given that the tax is not affecting market functioning in any manner, it is intriguing why Sebi is making such suggestions. Perhaps the market regulator is conveying its gleanings from conversations with FPIs and stakeholders. Be that as it may, the issue is worth debating. The outflow clearly has not happened because of taxes. It is worth highlighting that FPIs are buying too — it is just that the amount of selling is higher in the aggregate. For instance, FPIs have been net buyers thus far in November’s two days of trading, and were net buyers through July and August.  For policy purposes, the issue of recent FPI flows must be separated from that of taxation. Outflows are being driven by more fundamental factors, with implications for macroeconomic management. Risk capital from across the world is being invested in a big way in artificial intelligence (AI) and related areas. Since India is not a large player in AI, it is finding it difficult to attract foreign capital. The other reason is the significant increase in government bond yields across the world. An increase in the risk-free rate tends to push up the asking rate of return for other assets. These, along with higher oil prices owing to the conflict in West Asia, are putting pressure on the balance of payments and, consequently, the rupee.  Thus, the macroeconomic response to the situation needs to be much wider. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) attracted foreign flows under swap schemes, including one for Non-Resident Indians. The data suggests that it is using its reserves to contain the decline in the rupee. The RBI has also put various restrictions in the currency-derivatives market to curb volatility. However, these measures will work if global conditions are expected to turn favourable soon. If the underlying conditions persist for a few more months, macroeconomic management could become more challenging. A lot will depend on how the results of the midterm elections in the United States influence its actions in West Asia. On the issue of taxation, since India needs robust capital flows in all circumstances to supplement domestic savings to achieve higher economic growth, its policies should not be out of sync with the rest of the world. The government will have to consider various other aspects, such as taxing different instruments for resident investors. Ideally, differential tax treatment should not influence investment decisions unless that is the desired policy objective.     Topics : FPI outflow Foreign Portfolio Investors LTCG tax Nifty 50 Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!

A former Deputy Prime Minister and one of India's longest-serving Home Ministers, Lal Krishna Advani Ji is one of the few people whose lives have touched many different chapters of modern India

premium

Senior BJP leader LK Advani turns 99 today, marking the beginning of his 100th year.

Narendra Modi New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 6:00 AM ISTShri Lal Krishna Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life today, November 8. This year, his birthday fittingly coincides with Diwali, a festival associated with Prabhu Shri Ram and the diya at a time when we are marking 75 years since the inception of the Jana Sangh, the 125th Jayanti of Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee, and recently celebrated a hundred years of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).   There are very few people whose lives have touched so many different chapters of modern India. Advani Ji was born on November 8, 1927, on Dev Deepawali. As a youngster in 1947, he experienced the pain of leaving behind his familiar world in Sindh. He rebuilt his life from scratch without bitterness. This trait of being able to build from scratch, against all odds, has stayed with him throughout. It was seen while he was strengthening the Jana Sangh and later building the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). His tenures as BJP President saw the Congress falling sharply from 400 to below 200 in 1989 and the BJP becoming the single-largest party for the first time in 1996. Advani Ji nurtured generations of karyakartas and gave the party a clear foundation rooted in the principle of ‘Nation First’.   Two qualities always set Advani Ji apart as a leader. First, his ideological clarity and intellectual sharpness. This was reflected in his speeches and writings. The Jana Sangh and BJP resolutions he authored remain worth reading even today, while his interviews were consistently incisive and precise. Second, the manner in which he exposed the pseudo-secularism propounded by a large section of the Indian polity for many years.    Advani Ji took up every responsibility with immense diligence. As an RSS pracharak, Advani Ji first worked in different parts of Rajasthan. From there, he went to the national capital, where he started working closely with Atal Ji. History shows that it is rare for two towering political leaders to work together for several decades, cooperating with each other without becoming competitors. Advani Ji and Atal Ji set a remarkable example. Together, they changed the course of Indian politics.  The Delhi that Advani Ji came to was coming to terms with the horrors of Partition. He immersed himself in making the Jana Sangh stronger. In 1967, Advani Ji became the Chairman of the Delhi Metropolitan Council, where he worked alongside the late Vijay Kumar Malhotra Ji (who became Chief Executive Councillor).   In 1970, Advani Ji’s Parliamentary innings began. His interventions have won appreciation across the political spectrum. He made a mark as an Member of Parliament (MP) and later, as Leader of Opposition in both houses and from the treasury benches, too. Despite Parliamentary commitments, he frequently travelled across India meeting people.    I vividly recall the 1991 Lok Sabha elections. It was decided that Advani Ji would contest the Lok Sabha elections from two seats, one of which was Gandhinagar. He had an old link with Gujarat. His father had settled in Kutch after Partition. Advani Ji had also served as a Rajya Sabha MP from Gujarat. So, it was a homecoming of sorts. Being involved in the BJP organisation, I had the honour of helping prepare his papers and assisting him throughout the campaign. The people of Gandhinagar sent him to Parliament time and again. As a voter of Gandhinagar, I also had the honour of voting for Advani Ji on numerous occasions. The care and attention he devoted to his constituency is something to learn from.   The Emergency was a watershed moment in Advani Ji’s life. He was at the forefront of saving democracy and protecting the Constitution. His experiences found their way into his book, ‘A Prisoner's Scrap-Book.’ One part of that book, titled ‘A Tale of Two Emergencies’, beautifully explained the striking similarities between the events in India starting June 1975 and those in Nazi Germany in 1933.   Advani Ji was a fiery Opposition leader but an equally excellent administrator. When the Janata Government came to office in 1977, Advani Ji became Minister for Information and Broadcasting. It is widely accepted that his work in this department was extremely impactful. As Deputy Prime Minister and one of India’s longest-serving Home Ministers, he was instrumental in strengthening India’s security apparatus. His work in improving the lives of our security forces is remembered with great fondness. His unequivocal stand against terrorism ensured India got a tough anti-terror law.   Of course, an iconic moment in Advani Ji’s life was the Somnath to Ayodhya Rath Yatra. It changed the course of Indian society for the better. I consider it a privilege that I got the opportunity to be involved in this yatra from the ideation stage to execution. Being present at Somnath when the yatra began was particularly special. A yatra can be very demanding, requiring long hours, constant travel, physical endurance and an ability to remain focused despite fatigue. Advani Ji embodied this endurance.  I also have memories of the saddening moments of Advani Ji’s arrest in Bihar. Then, in Gujarat, the BJP withdrew support from the Chimanbhai Patel government. With this, a simple message was given, that when it comes to our ideology and the Ram Temple, there will never be any compromise. Many of our senior leaders and karyakartas took an oath that, come what may, a Ram Temple will be built. And, years later, with the blessings of the people of India, a grand Mandir for Prabhu Shri Ram became a reality in Ayodhya.   There is so much more of Advani Ji that is outstanding. His simplicity, for example. After the Navnirman Movement, Advani Ji had come to Junagadh and stayed for a month as an ordinary karyakarta, preparing the party for the Assembly elections in which the Congress was rejected. He has always shown what probity in public life is about. He is a voracious reader. Those who have spent time with him know how carefully he goes through newspapers. He is a big fan of cinema and theatre, and has been an enthusiastic film critic. His sense of history and the need to preserve it is visible in his book, ‘My Country My Life’.  Advani Ji always remained in touch with Sindhi culture. Another effort he undertook was the popularisation of Sindhu Darshan Puja near Leh. I myself have been to one puja with Advani Ji and George Fernandes Ji.   Any account of Advani Ji’s remarkable journey would be incomplete without mentioning Kamla Advani Ji. She was a constant source of strength and support throughout his public life.  Growing up in Karachi, Advani Ji could hardly have imagined the path his life would take. In an expression of gratitude, the people of India conferred upon him the Bharat Ratna in 2024. As Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life, I pray that he be blessed with good health and that he continues to inspire us all as he has always done.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Narendra Modi LK Advani Bharat Ratna

entry.title: A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultationA 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation

Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government erred in taking its most loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi-heartland farmers and soldiers

Representative Picture

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 07 2026 | 11:53 AM ISTYou can find a more diplomatic or politically convenient description for it, but the Modi government’s latest move on the Agniveer scheme, brought in with such aplomb, is a rollback. More so, a poll-eve capitulation. Seventy-five per cent of the first lot of Agniveers would have finished their tour of duty, or walked the Agnipath (path of fire), as the scheme was named, and returned to their hometowns and villages by December. It’s just that many would have gone back to Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab, even Manipur, all going to the polls this coming February. All are traditionally major catchment areas for armed forces recruitment. For the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the first two are much too vital to risk.  The prospect of these demobilised soldiers returning and joining opposition rallies, even enrolling in something like the Cockroach Janta Party, was scary for the BJP which, until the other day, was riding an all-conquering confidence. Now, it was seen as a risk not worth taking. On top of these, in November or thereabouts next year, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat will have their state elections. Gujarat, the BJP can still be calm about. But Himachal, a stronghold it lost to the Congress last time, is a traditional recruiting area with a large ex-servicemen’s constituency.

Also Read

Why cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to Indiapremium

How India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voicepremium

Amid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK Shivakumarpremium

CR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and recordspremium

Agniveer cadets get two-year extension as Cabinet approves tenure hike

 The party has now become far too risk-averse to put to the electoral test what was once its favourite reform. Reform it was, though. And we’ll talk about how, and then why it collapsed at its first test. There are three things governments are remembered for. Then there’s a fourth category: The good ideas a government implements and then withdraws under pressure or in panic. The good and the bad ideas are the first two. The third is the good ideas they propose but lack the nerve or skills to implement. We can list many of the United Progressive Alliance’s (UPA’s), for example: Aadhaar and India Stack based on it, direct benefit transfer (DBT) of welfare, even targeted delivery of subsidised cooking gas only to the poor and deserving. So were its many grand and audacious infrastructure projects of national importance. All got caught either in its indecision loop, internal party-versus-government contradictions, or ideological opposition. Most were subsequently consummated by the Modi government. Think the rail link to Srinagar, Mumbai Metro, Trans Harbour Link, the new Expressways, completion of the dedicated freight corridors (DFCs) and even the annihilation of armed Maoism. All of these were UPA projects abandoned midway. The Modi government did a brilliant job with these. It just tripped up on some of its own ideas. In journalism, we follow the three-example rule, meaning that these make a straight line. Or your argument. For Modi government’s rollbacks, count the farm laws, brought in with such self-assurance in 2020 and rolled back in their entirety in 2021 in the face of opposition from farmers. The second is now the Agniveer scheme. For the third, my preference would be the caste Census. The Modi government was opposed to it forever, then suddenly included it in the delayed 2021 Census being carried out now. This was under Rahul Gandhi’s pressure. If you don’t think that’s strong enough to make the third example —although I think it does, given the implications — I can give you another. The Prime Minister repeatedly derided the freebie culture, or what he contemptuously dismissed as “revdi” culture. Speaking at the inauguration of the Bundelkhand Expressway at Jalaun in UP in July 2022, he said, “This revdi culture is very dangerous for the development of the country. Those with revdi culture will never build new expressways, new airports or defence corridors for you.” And then, around the time of the Chhattisgarh elections in the winter of 2023, he announced that the Covid-era free food grain scheme would continue. In the same set of elections, the BJP brought in the Ladli Behna Yojana for cash transfers to women. Then, probably stung by the loss of majority in 2024, the party unleashed an almighty revdi “revolution”, with payouts reaching up to  ₹10,000 as a one-time transfer in Bihar and a promise of  ₹2 lakh if the woman started an enterprise. This was so expensive that even a rich state like Maharashtra is struggling to pay out, looking for excuses to reduce the number of beneficiaries. Women are already protesting, saying they’ve been denied their “Ladki Bahin” payouts. If you prefer, you can list this as the third example. However you look at it, this government has lost much of its appetite for risk, even with reforms where it had shown great conviction and commitment. These four examples are enough to show that the Modi government will also be remembered for the really good ideas it brought in, Agnipath included, and rolled back. This column, for the record, had supported each of these ideas. Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government failed the test of both elements of the “ Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan” sentiment. It erred in taking its most significant and loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi heartland farmers and soldiers. The most disappointing thing is how it failed to reach out to them and build acceptance for such radical changes. People are by and large suspicious of major policy shifts with such significant implications for their lives, particularly when introduced through a shock-and-awe approach. That, however, has been this government’s style. Think sudden demonetisation or the Covid lockdown. Decisions affecting farmers and soldiers were taken in much the same way. Unlike the first two, which came with an end date, these policy changes were meant to survive in perpetuity. That explains the pushback from the base, and the Modi government’s rollback. Governance remains a painstaking, laborious, even boring business because it requires background work, scenario-mapping, war-gaming, or what the armed forces would call staff work. That is what the civil services and bureaucracies are there for. The absence of this precise element has bedevilled these plans — surprising, given how heavily the Modi government depends on civil servants. Were they asked to do their homework, or handed the decision first? There may be a concern that decisions could get caught in an analysis-paralysis loop. But you can’t always be like a commando who jumps out of a plane without checking the parachute. That isn’t fearless. It’s reckless. When Agnipath was implemented, it was well known that the first lot would leave on the eve of these state elections. An extensive rehabilitation programme, beginning midway through their four years, could have cushioned the blow. Now, the baby is gone, and with it the bathwater. The same lack of homework preceded the implementation of One Rank, One Pension (OROP). It was an election promise, all parties agreed with it, and no Indian would begrudge soldiers this benefit. But if the additional costs had been calculated and a necessary top-up provided to the defence budget, the story might have been different. The sudden increase in pensions because of OROP came from a defence budget that didn’t even keep pace with inflation over the years. This shrank the capital or acquisition budget. As concerns grew, Agnipath was rolled out in a hurry. Poor staff work created two kinds of soldiers, two sets of wages and even two sets of benefits for families in the event of a battle fatality. Most significant armies now have soldiers serving short tenures. But they don’t treat conscripted soldiers as a category separate from those on full-career service. Here, they were even addressed separately. Each unit then had an Agniveer sub-unit within it. This was unsustainable. The twin ideas of reducing the pension burden going ahead and making the armed forces much younger were both virtuous. Both have been lost to poor planning, hasty implementation and now withdrawal. This first batch will finish its sixth year on the eve of the 2029 general election. Rescuing this good idea will be a political miracle. It’s looking like a case of na khuda hi mila, na visaal-e-sanam (neither did I find God, nor my beloved).

entry.title: Buildup to the day of 'infamy'
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Buildup to the day of 'infamy'Buildup to the day of 'infamy'

How Tata Trusts' unity began to unravel soon after Ratan Tata's death, leading to the turmoil of September

premium

Differences between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons have intensified since Ratan Tata’s death, with disagreements over leadership and the holding company’s proposed listing culminating in the September 17 boardroom turmoil.

Nivedita Mookerji5 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 10:38 PM ISTSenior advocate Darius Khambata, while announcing his exit from Tata Trusts, asked a pertinent question — would September 17 have happened if Ratan Tata had been around? Calling it a day of “infamy”, Mr Khambata answered himself: Of course not. But, there’s a question that Mr Khambata’s letter missed asking: Would the events leading up to September 17 have happened if Ratan Tata, who was chairman of Tata Trusts — the largest shareholder of Tata Sons with a 66 per cent stake — for over 30 years and a trustee for 60 years, had been around?  February 2026 is when the rift between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons became public for the first time. It’s been more than eight months since Bombay House — headquarters of Tata Sons — has remained unsure and unsettled. On February 24, at a Tata Sons board meeting, Noel Tata questioned N Chandrasekaran on the financials of certain companies, including Air India. Noel, with a 1 per cent share in Tata Sons and chairman of Tata Trusts since October 11, 2024 (two days after his half-brother Ratan Tata died), was resisting a third term for Mr Chandrasekaran. At that time, Noel was 15 months into the role as a nominee director of Tata Trusts on the Tata Sons board.  Incidentally, Noel became the first person in more than a decade to be both Tata Trusts chairman and a member of the Tata Sons board. Tata Sons amended its Articles of Association (AoA) in 2022 to mandate that the chairman of Tata Sons and the chairman of Tata Trusts cannot be the same person, to prevent excessive concentration of power in one individual.  Ratan Tata was the last one to hold both the positions simultaneously until his retirement in 2012.  During the February 2026 board meeting, Mr Chandrasekaran, who had by then clocked nine years as Tata Sons chairman, wanted the directors to put on hold the deliberations on his third term until a consensus emerged. It never did in the months that followed, culminating in the September 17 board meeting, where Noel opposed the resolution on Mr Chandrasekaran’s reappointment. Not too long ago, in July 2025, Tata Trusts had unanimously passed a resolution backing a five-year third term for Mr Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of Tata Sons to ensure continuity at a time when the group was investing in new businesses. Both items in the Tata Trusts resolution of July 2025 — Mr Chandrasekaran’s third term and the listing of Tata Sons — were taken up by the Tata Sons board on September 17, 2026 — the day of “infamy” as Mr Khambata put it. Both have remained subjects of intense dispute.  Mr Chandrasekaran’s second term comes to an end on February 20, 2027, and while the Tata Sons board approved a third term for him on September 17, the future still hangs in the balance. The letter that he wrote to the Tata Sons board on August 12, 2026, stating that he would not seek reappointment as chairman of Tata Sons due to a lack of unanimous support, suggesting Noel’s opposition, may have added to the complexity of the situation. More so, because he acceded to the Tata Sons board resolution a month later on September 17 granting him a third term despite a lack of unanimous support. The age of retirement, at 65 years, for Tata group executives has also been a thorny issue. Mr Chandrasekaran will turn 65 in June 2028, that’s 16 months into his third term, if it happens. Ratan Tata had stepped down as executive chairman of Tata Sons when he turned 65 in 2002 and then continued as non-executive chairman for another 10 years with several major deals struck during the latter stint.  As for the listing of Tata Sons, the July 2025 resolution of Tata Trusts had decided that all efforts should be made to ensure that the holding company remained privately held. The September 2026 Tata Sons board meeting decided to go ahead with a stock exchange listing of Tata Sons, after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected its application made in 2024 to deregister itself as a core investment company. The RBI letter dated September 11— six days before the September 17 Tata Sons board meeting — changed the trajectory of things, making stock market listing mandatory for the company. To put things in context, the RBI had placed Tata Sons, among others, on the list of upper-layer non-banking financial company in September 2022, mandating a listing within three years. Tata Sons cleared all its debt and applied to the RBI in March 2024 for deregistration and, therefore, an exemption from listing. The RBI reply — a rejection came 30 months after the Tata Sons application. While Noel Tata has proposed a restructuring of Tata Sons to avoid a listing, the status of that proposal in the regulatory ecosystem is hazy.  In the sequence of things, while Tata Sons versus Tata Trusts has dominated the India Inc conversation in the last few months, the in-fighting within Tata Trusts, a tax-exempt charitable organisation, had started within months of Ratan Tata’s passing. Negative voting for routine renewals became a regular occurrence, resulting in disputes as well as intervention of the authorities ranging from the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner to ministers.        The current impasse has come a decade after the boardroom coup steered by Ratan Tata to remove Cyrus Mistry as the chairman of Tata Sons on October 24, 2016. Whether or not October 24, 2016, was a day of ‘infamy’ too, Tata Trusts under Ratan Tata was seen as an organisation that stood together. That changed soon after his death, leading to the turmoil of September.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India can't afford to ignore money growth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India can't afford to ignore money growthIndia can't afford to ignore money growth

With inflation expectations difficult to measure in India's context, monetary aggregates offer a valuable cross-check

premium

Reserve bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Prasanna Tantri5 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:34 PM IST“Similarly, there are risks of demand-side pressures in view of the growth in monetary and credit aggregates.” This sentence from the Reserve Bank of India Governor in the latest Monetary Policy Committee minutes deserves attention. After receding from public-policy discussions, the quantity of money is receiving explicit recognition once again. Should we bother with it when the RBI already sets interest rates and targets inflation? In India, the answer is yes.  The numbers explain why. Broad money, or M3, consists principally of currency and bank deposits. Its growth accelerated from around 9.3 per cent in 2024-25 to 15.3 per cent in 2025-26, while nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grew by less than 9 per cent in the latter year. Annual money growth remained at 16 per cent on October 15. Our compilation places M3 at approximately 91 per cent of GDP in March and around 93 per cent by September, using projected GDP. The ratio was approximately 86 per cent 18 months earlier. This represents substantial monetary expansion relative to income.  There is, however, a serious intellectual argument against assigning money growth an independent role in policymaking. In the New Keynesian framework associated with the recent Nobel prize winners, spending responds to current and expected future real interest rates. The relevant real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation. Lower real rates encourage spending today and weaken the incentive to postpone consumption. When prices adjust slowly, stronger demand eventually pushes up inflation.  From this perspective, monetary policy works through interest rates, expectations, and financing conditions. The central bank need not separately target money if these channels adequately capture the stance. Money may expand because banks lend more and create deposits, making it partly an outcome of economic decisions rather than an independent cause. Financial innovation also makes money difficult to define, while the central bank cannot precisely control broad money.  Moreover, creating bank reserves does not guarantee additional lending. Banks may retain liquid assets because they fear losses, lack capital or cannot find creditworthy customers. Borrowers may prefer repayment to fresh borrowing. The American experience after the global financial crisis illustrates why reserve creation need not translate proportionately into money, credit or inflation.  Monetarists would respond that this places too much confidence in policymakers’ ability to identify the correct interest rate. A nominal rate can look restrictive while being expansionary once expected inflation is factored in. Sustained growth in money beyond the public’s willingness to hold it encourages adjustment through spending and purchases of assets. Money, therefore, provides information that an interest-rate diagnosis can miss. The relationship is neither immediate nor mechanically proportional: Desired money holdings and the speed of spending also change.  India has two reasons to take this monetarist warning seriously.  First, the possibility that additional liquidity remains disconnected from lending is less reassuring when credit is already expanding strongly. Bank credit reached ₹227.43 trillion on October 15, growing 18.2 per cent over the preceding year, compared with 11.6 per cent a year earlier. This does not establish that reserve creation caused every additional loan. It establishes that we are not observing abundant reserves alongside stagnant bank lending. Money and credit are expanding together.  Second, and more importantly, India lacks a sufficiently reliable measure of the inflation expectations driving spending, saving and price-setting. Household survey expectations persistently exceed subsequent national consumer price index-based inflation. Some discrepancy reflects households’ different consumption baskets. Survey movements can still be informative. But using these numerical expectations to calculate the real rate remains problematic.  Professional forecasts help predict reported inflation, but they cannot substitute for understanding the expectations governing wage negotiations, rents, school fees and contract renewals. Those decisions determine how anticipated inflation enters future prices. We need better surveys and evidence from contracts committing parties to future payments.  Until then, monetary aggregates offer a valuable cross-check. Even someone convinced that money has no independent causal role should ask whether its growth improves inflation forecasts. Prediction does not require establishing that the predictor independently causes the outcome. If money growth helps anticipate inflation, ignoring it because causality is disputed would discard useful information.  This is compatible with a New Keynesian framework. If expected inflation is mismeasured, our estimate of the real rate is wrong. Rapid monetary and credit growth should prompt a reassessment: Is policy providing more stimulus than the nominal repo rate suggests?  Nor is all monetary growth dangerous. A growing economy needs more money, and financial deepening can justify a higher money-to-GDP ratio. The warning is persistent, substantial expansion beyond income growth without evidence of a corresponding increase in desired money holdings.  India’s historical experience suggests that 80-84 per cent of GDP is a useful reference range for broad money, not a scientifically established optimum. Returning towards it gradually would require money growth to lag nominal income growth, rather than an abrupt monetary contraction.  The repo rate should remain the principal instrument and inflation the objective. But money growth deserves an explicit place in forecasts, minutes and communication. When expectations are poorly measured, an interest-rate framework needs more cross-checks, not fewer.

entry.title: A relook at food subsidy
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A relook at food subsidyA relook at food subsidy

Estimates on poverty reduction should be used to usher in a targeted scheme for free foodgrain

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTLess than three months are left before the Union Budget for 2027-28 is due to be presented in Parliament. Even as inter-ministerial consultations have started and discussions with representatives of industry, trade, and farmers, among others, are set to be held soon, expectations from the forthcoming Budget are already running high. This is not just because the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has called for the removal of the long-term capital gains tax for foreign portfolio investors, but also because Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has responded to this issue by making a careful statement that the government acknowledges concerns about sustained foreign investment inflows and the market’s anxiety over them.  Expectedly, the stock market has responded positively to these statements in the hope that the Union Budget on February 1 will revise the taxation framework for long-term capital gains from assets. At another level, senior government officials are making statements that underline the need for more reforms. Those too have raised expectations from the forthcoming Budget.  Last week, Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) V Anantha Nageswaran delivered an important address highlighting the imperatives before India’s economic policymakers in the face of the current challenges. For obvious reasons, the headline for the CEA’s address focused on the comparison between the current economic challenges of 2026 and those that India faced in 1991. Of course, the comparison was qualified, even though the structural and external challenges were as formidable then as they are now. The policy suggestions made by the CEA, particularly the one requiring a re-examination of the country’s growth and industrial strategies, deserve serious consideration. The simultaneous pursuit of import substitution, stronger local manufacturing, and improved export competitiveness will also require a reimagined policy approach.  Similarly, recent statements from Niti Aayog Member Rajiv Gauba have ignited hopes of an overhaul of urban governance, with empowered city governments, directly elected mayors with five-year terms, greater financial autonomy for urban local bodies, and the introduction of integrated land-use planning in cities and towns of India. Over the past many years, the Union Budget has gone beyond fiscal matters, outlining the government’s overall development policies as well. Mr Gauba’s statement that urban centres cannot be effectively run from state Capitals should lead to necessary governance reforms, as city governments will require the authority, resources and institutional capacity to address local developmental issues.  The coming Union Budget can lay down a road map for ensuring the devolvement of all 18 functions, listed under the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act to urban local bodies. States can be nudged to ensure that urban local bodies are empowered to take decisions on master planning, water supply, fire services, and traffic management, which are all functions currently controlled by most state governments.  But going beyond governance, there is an important issue that the Union Budget should tackle to support the government’s fiscal situation. That reform should be in the area of food subsidies and its need has been triggered by a World Bank report (the Poverty and Equity Brief for India) released in October. It states that between 2011 and 2023, the share of Indians living below the poverty line, using the yardstick for lower middle-income countries (daily consumption of $4.2), fell from 57.7 per cent to 16.1 per cent. The World Bank report released another datapoint indicating that India’s extreme poverty (measured by a daily consumption of $3, used for low-income countries) fell from 27.1 per cent to 2.6 per cent during the same period. But the relevant number for India’s poverty estimate is the one showing the decline in the share of poor people in the country’s total population to 16.1 per cent. India is a lower middle-income country and the daily consumption benchmark of $4.2 is the correct yardstick to measure India’s poverty level.  Such a reduction in India’s poverty level is obviously being debated among economists. There are many questions about how this reduction was achieved and whether it impacted the level of inequality in India. While these issues warrant further discussion, another policy debate should be triggered by this poverty reduction. This is about the Modi government’s scheme to supply free foodgrain to over 800 million Indians.  Remember that India did not have a free foodgrain scheme in 2011, when its poverty level was 57.7 per cent, according to the World Bank. The free foodgrain scheme was started in March 2020 in response to the Covid pandemic. It was tweaked slightly to cover all beneficiaries under the National Food Security Act in January 2023 for a period of 12 months, even though Covid was no longer a threat at that time. Then, a few weeks before January 2024, it was announced that the free foodgrain scheme would run for five years. In the process, over 57 per cent of India’ total population has come to enjoy free foodgrain, even though the country has a poverty rate of 16 per cent.  For the Union government, the free foodgrain scheme entails a significant cost. Food subsidies are estimated at over ₹2 trillion every year, over four per cent of the government’s total annual expenditure. Food subsidies cannot be completely eliminated. But they can certainly be reduced significantly if the free foodgrain scheme is targeted to benefit only the poor. Any such move will face obvious political pushback because of the electoral costs it could impose on the ruling party.  But a government that could take on powerful retailers by reintroducing the merchant discount rate (MDR) on select transactions made through the Unified Payments Interface can be expected to roll out a similar free foodgrain scheme that benefits only the poor and needy.  Why talk of only traders? The government this year has successfully linked the sale of fertilisers to farmers’ land records through the use of AgriStack and other digital platforms. Fertiliser sales this kharif season fell by over 37 per cent. As a result, the new scheme has prevented large-scale diversion of fertilisers to non-farming sectors and to neighbouring countries, where fertiliser prices are much higher. The government’s fertiliser subsidies bill too has benefitted.  Hopefully, the proposed MDR will be enforced after Diwali, and the scheme linking fertiliser sales to land records will be continued and expanded to cover more farmers after addressing concerns of tenant farmers. Food and fertiliser subsidies in the first half of the current financial year have been kept under check so far, growing by 13 per cent against the annual growth projection of 18 per cent. Given the way energy prices have been behaving, the government needs to introduce these subsidy reforms to provide some cushion against expenditure slippages in other areas this year and during 2027-28.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
